challenges.situation: You've been helping a colleague for months — covering their gaps, sharing your research. They keep taking without reciprocating. A friend says 'stop being nice.' What does Tit-for-Tat actually prescribe?

options.text: Stop helping them next time they ask (punish), but if they start reciprocating, immediately return to helping (forgive)
options.feedback: Tit-for-Tat is retaliatory AND forgiving. It punishes defection immediately (stop helping next time) but doesn't hold grudges — if they start reciprocating, you return to cooperation. Permanent cutoff is too harsh (locks in mutual defection). Indefinite tolerance is too soft (signals that exploitation has no consequences). Public escalation introduces noise.

options.text: Cut them off permanently — they've shown their true character
options.feedback: Not quite. Tit-for-Tat is retaliatory AND forgiving. It punishes defection immediately (stop helping next time) but doesn't hold grudges — if they start reciprocating, you return to cooperation.

options.text: Keep helping anyway because the relationship is long-term and they might come around eventually
options.feedback: Not quite. Tit-for-Tat is retaliatory AND forgiving. It punishes defection immediately (stop helping next time) but doesn't hold grudges — if they start reciprocating, you return to cooperation.

options.text: Escalate by publicly calling out their behavior to create social pressure
options.feedback: Not quite. Tit-for-Tat is retaliatory AND forgiving. It punishes defection immediately (stop helping next time) but doesn't hold grudges — if they start reciprocating, you return to cooperation.

challenges.situation: In Axelrod's tournament, 'always defect' strategies scored well in individual rounds but lost overall. Complex strategies that mixed cooperation and defection also lost.
challenges.question: What made Tit-for-Tat's simplicity its superpower?

options.text: Trust — its predictable pattern let opponents feel safe cooperating, triggering mutual gain across hundreds of rounds
options.feedback: Tit-for-Tat's clarity created trust. When opponents could instantly predict 'if I cooperate, it cooperates back,' they chose cooperation — because the safe path was also the profitable one. Complex strategies failed because opponents couldn't build stable expectations, so they defaulted to self-protection. Readability enables trust.

options.text: Fear — opponents feared its retaliation and never tried to exploit it
options.feedback: Not quite. Tit-for-Tat's clarity created trust. When opponents could instantly predict 'if I cooperate, it cooperates back,' they chose cooperation — because the safe path was also the profitable one.

options.text: Status — being known as the tournament winner gave it an advantage in later rounds
options.feedback: Not quite. Tit-for-Tat's clarity created trust. When opponents could instantly predict 'if I cooperate, it cooperates back,' they chose cooperation — because the safe path was also the profitable one.

options.text: Incentives — the point system naturally rewarded simple strategies over complex ones

challenges.instruction: Match each concept to its description:

pairs.right: Infinite repeated game with total reputation visibility

pairs.left: Online marketplace with anonymous one-time sellers
pairs.right: One-shot game where defection (fraud) is rational

pairs.left: Colleague who is sometimes generous, sometimes cold
pairs.right: Unpredictable strategy that destroys trust conditions

pairs.left: Rotating WWI soldiers to prevent truces
pairs.right: Converting a repeated game into one-shot interactions

pairs.left: Community expelling a cheating trader permanently
pairs.right: Making defection cost exceed any possible single-round gain

challenges.context: Which response shows better understanding of the underlying dynamics?

scenarioA.label: Naive or Cynical
scenarioA.text: Either I'm generous without boundaries (and get exploited) or I'm protective without generosity (and miss every opportunity for cooperation). Nice guys finish last.

scenarioB.label: Strategic Generosity
scenarioB.text: I cooperate first. I punish defection immediately. I forgive after one punishment. I make my pattern crystal clear. I'm not nice or tough — I'm readable. And readable wins in every repeated game.

challenges.explanation: The stronger response reads the game as repeated and plays the winning pattern: cooperate first, retaliate against defection immediately, then forgive — rather than being unconditionally nice or tough.

principle.text: The most important question in any interaction isn't "what should I do?" It's "what kind of game am I in?"
principle.subtext: In one-shot games (you'll never see this person again), being generous is exploitable. In repeated games (you'll interact again and again), being generous is the foundation of the strongest strategy ever tested.

reflection: In your most important repeated relationship (work or personal), are you being 'nice, retaliating, and forgiving' — or are you holding grudges that block return to cooperation?
